name: Mesenchymal stem cell conditioned media

lead: Mesenchymal stem cell conditioned media is the liquid in which stem cells have grown, containing the growth factors and vesicles they secrete. It appears in serums and post-procedure treatments for skin regeneration and a smoother, rejuvenated look.

The secreted factors are thought to signal nearby cells, for example promoting fibroblast migration and dampening inflammation in cell models. Most research is lab and animal wound-healing work, and early-phase human trials are registered for conditions such as chronic ulcers and keloids.

paras: Applied as a serum, often after microneedling or other procedures, as a cell-free alternative to stem cell therapy.
Composition varies between preparations. A laboratory study reported MSC-derived chemokines promoting tumor-cell invasion, and no long-term cosmetic safety data were found in the sources reviewed.

angle.text: Stem-cell conditioned media carry growth factors and vesicles meant to signal skin repair and collagen support for smoother, rejuvenated skin. Lab and animal work is extensive, and human trials are early-phase.

lead: Mesenchymal stem cell conditioned media (MSC-CM), also called the MSC secretome, is the liquid in which mesenchymal stem cells have been grown, containing the proteins, growth factors, vesicles and other molecules they release.[1][2] Versions made from adipose-derived stem cells (ADSC-CM) are among those studied. Products based on it are marketed in serums and post-procedure treatments for regeneration.

Most of the published research is laboratory or animal work on wound healing and inflammation, and reviews describe it as a possible cell-free alternative to stem cell therapy.[3][4] Early-phase human trials are registered for conditions such as chronic ulcers and keloids; the sources reviewed here do not report their results.[5][6]

paras: The secretome is the set of proteins cells release outside themselves, including cytokines and growth factors; cells also release RNA and lipids in vesicles.[7] Conditioned media captures this mixture from cultured cells without containing the cells themselves, and a 2021 narrative review discusses its regenerative potential and the barriers to clinical translation.[2]

Registered human trials found in the sources are early-phase. They include a completed phase 1 study of conditioned medium on chronic ulcer wounds (38 participants),[5] a phase 1/2 trial comparing MSC, conditioned medium or triamcinolone for keloid,[6] and a phase 1 study of a conditioned-medium-derived factor for skin graft donor sites.[8] The registrations reviewed do not include results, and no trial of cosmetic serums is described.

A 2018 study found that adipose-derived stem cell conditioned media and exosomes containing the long noncoding RNA MALAT1 promoted migration of human dermal fibroblasts and wound healing in an ischemic wound model.[1] A 2022 cell study reported that MSC-conditioned media reduced activation of macrophages exposed to a bacterial toxin.[4] A 2020 review described it as a possible alternative to stem cell therapy for wound healing.[3]

A 2013 laboratory study reported that MSC-derived chemokines promoted mammary tumor cell invasion, illustrating that secreted factors can have effects not limited to repair.[9] Safety data in people in the sources reviewed are limited to small early-phase trials without published results.
